body:
Understanding the Harappan Civilisation

The Harappan Civilisation, also known as the Indus Civilisation, was a Bronze Age civilisation that developed across northwestern parts of the Indian subcontinent and adjoining regions. It is named after Harappa, in present-day Pakistan, one of the first major sites to be excavated.

The civilisation did not appear suddenly as a collection of large cities. Agricultural settlements, regional cultures and small towns developed over many centuries. Some of these settlements eventually became part of an extensive urban civilisation. Later, as large cities declined, people continued living in smaller settlements and developed regional cultural traditions.

Early Harappan refers broadly to the period of settlement growth before mature urbanisation; Mature Harappan refers to the main period of developed cities; and Late Harappan refers to the period when the earlier urban system weakened and regional settlement traditions became more prominent.

The three principal phases

Early Harappan: approximately 3300–2600 BCE

This was the formative period. Farming and animal husbandry supported villages and growing towns. Communities made pottery, developed crafts and exchanged goods with other settlements. Different regions had distinctive pottery and building traditions rather than a fully uniform urban culture.

Some features later associated with Mature Harappan civilisation, including fortified settlements and improved town planning, began to develop during this broad period. However, the extensive network of large, similarly organised cities had not yet reached its mature form.

Mature Harappan: approximately 2600–1900 BCE

This was the main urban phase. Large cities and smaller settlements participated in an interconnected cultural and economic system. Many sites shared characteristic seals, standardised weights, pottery, beads, bricks and writing. Planned streets, drainage arrangements and specialised crafts distinguished major urban centres.

The Mature Harappan phase is also the period referred to when textbooks give the core dates of the developed Harappan civilisation as 2600–1900 BCE. These dates do not mean that all Harappan communities existed only during those centuries.

Late Harappan: approximately 1900–1300 BCE

After approximately 1900 BCE, several large urban centres declined or were abandoned, while many smaller settlements continued to be occupied. The widespread use of characteristic seals, writing, standardised weights and certain specialised crafts diminished. Regional pottery traditions became more prominent.

Settlement patterns also changed. Some regions, particularly parts of Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, received new or continuing populations even while major urban centres elsewhere declined. The decline of large Harappan cities was not the disappearance of every Harappan community.

Why the dates are approximate

The three-phase division is a useful historical framework, not a statement that every settlement changed on the same day. Different textbooks and studies may use somewhat different dates for the Early and Late phases or identify additional transitional stages. The boundary between Mature and Late Harappan culture is conventionally placed at about 1900 BCE.

Remember that BCE dates count backwards towards the Common Era: 3300 BCE is earlier than 2600 BCE, which is earlier than 1900 BCE.

Why the urban phase declined

Changes in river courses, reduced water availability, flooding and environmental pressures have been suggested as contributing factors in different regions. No single proposed cause adequately explains changes at every site. The clearest overall result was a transition from a widely connected urban system to more varied regional settlements.

Prelims focus

  • Early Harappan: approximately 3300–2600 BCE.
  • Mature Harappan: approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
  • Late Harappan: approximately 1900–1300 BCE.
  • The Mature phase is associated with developed cities, seals, writing and standardised weights.
  • After approximately 1900 BCE, urban decline was accompanied by the continuation and growth of regional settlements.
  • Trap: The end of the Mature Harappan phase does not mean that all Harappan sites were abandoned in 1900 BCE.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 1–2, 17; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation, pp. 88–90; Harappa.com, Timeline, consulted 17 November 2026.]

body:
A civilisation extending beyond the Indus Valley

The Harappan Civilisation was not confined to the valley of the Indus River. Its settlements spread across different river systems, plains, dry regions and coastal areas. The name Indus Valley Civilisation reflects its early discovery history, but the wider term Harappan Civilisation is useful when studying its full geographical distribution.

Major Harappan settlements were located in territories that now belong to Pakistan and India. The wider cultural and exchange network also extended into Afghanistan. Present-day political boundaries did not exist during the Harappan period.

The principal geographical clusters

Indus and its tributaries

The Indus system supported major settlements in the Punjab and Sindh regions. Harappa is in present-day Punjab, Pakistan, while Mohenjodaro is in Sindh, Pakistan. These sites provide the best-known examples of Mature Harappan urban development.

Ghaggar-Hakra and neighbouring plains

Many Harappan settlements occupied the plains of present-day Haryana and Rajasthan and adjoining areas of Pakistan. The Ghaggar-Hakra system is an important geographical reference for this distribution.

Three sites in this broad cluster are especially useful for identifying different kinds of evidence: Banawali in Haryana, known for a terracotta plough model; Rakhigarhi in Haryana, known for its extensive settlement remains; and Kalibangan in Rajasthan, known for an ancient ploughed field and later Harappan structures.

Sutlej region of Punjab

Ropar, also called Rupnagar, is situated on the Sutlej River in present-day Punjab, India. Its Harappan remains demonstrate that settlement activity extended into the eastern Punjab region.

Gujarat: Kutch and Saurashtra

Gujarat formed an important southern and western part of the Harappan settlement region. Its archaeological sites show both shared Harappan features and distinctive local traditions.

Surkotada is in Kutch and is associated with a fortified Harappan settlement. Rangpur and Rojdi are in Saurashtra. Their remains are particularly useful for understanding regional pottery traditions and the continuation of settlements beyond the main urban phase.

The Afghanistan connection

Shortughai, in present-day Afghanistan, shows that Harappan connections reached far beyond the Indus plains. It lay near a source of lapis lazuli, a valued blue stone, and traces of canals have been identified at the site.

Shortughai must be identified by its modern country, Afghanistan, rather than by an Indian state.

Understanding the regional pattern

The distribution of sites helps explain why Harappan settlements were not all identical. Communities living beside major rivers, along the Ghaggar-Hakra system, in Kutch and Saurashtra, or near distant sources of valuable stone faced different local conditions. Nevertheless, many participated in a wider network of exchange and shared cultural practices.

For example, Shortughai is important for its distant location and canals, while Rojdi is important for its regional settlement and pottery traditions. Their different characteristics do not make either site unrelated to the Harappan world.

Prelims focus

  • Shortughai is in present-day Afghanistan.
  • Banawali and Rakhigarhi are in Haryana.
  • Kalibangan is in Rajasthan.
  • Ropar or Rupnagar is in Punjab, India, near the Sutlej.
  • Surkotada, Rangpur and Rojdi are in Gujarat.
  • Trap: Harappan settlement was not restricted to the Indus River valley or to the territory of present-day Pakistan.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, pp. 1–3, Maps 1–2; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 88–91; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, map preceding p. 9; GCERT, History, Standard 11, Chapter 2, Harappan Civilisation, pp. 7–8.]
title: Geographical Spread: Harappan Regions and Site Clusters

body:
Three different types of agricultural evidence

A model of a farming tool, marks left by actual cultivation and traces of a water channel provide different kinds of information. The distinction is important when identifying Harappan sites from their discoveries.

Banawali is associated with a model of a plough, Kalibangan with a ploughed field, and Shortughai with canal traces. These discoveries are related to agriculture, but they are not interchangeable.

Banawali, Haryana: a terracotta plough model

Banawali is situated in present-day Fatehabad district, Haryana. The site has evidence of Early Harappan, Mature Harappan and later occupation.

A notable discovery is a terracotta model of a plough. Terracotta means clay that has been shaped and fired. The model indicates familiarity with a plough as an agricultural implement used to turn or loosen soil before sowing.

The distinction is that archaeologists discovered a model, not a surviving full-sized wooden plough. The model supports an understanding of agricultural technology without proving the exact design of every plough used by the Harappans.

Kalibangan, Rajasthan: a field with crossing furrows

Kalibangan lies in present-day Hanumangarh district, Rajasthan, beside the dry course of the Ghaggar River. Excavations revealed both an earlier settlement and a later Mature Harappan town.

Its most distinctive agricultural find is an ancient ploughed field. The field preserves 2 sets of furrows crossing at right angles. A furrow is a long, narrow groove made in cultivated soil, commonly by a plough.

The 2 directions of the furrows suggest that different crops may have been grown together in the same field. This interpretation is plausible because the differently spaced rows could accommodate different plants, but the preserved furrows alone do not identify the exact crops.

Chronological distinction: The famous ploughed field at Kalibangan belongs to its Early Harappan or pre-Mature Harappan occupation. The site also contained a later Mature Harappan settlement. The presence of both phases at one site must not be confused with the date of the ploughed field itself.

Fire altars at Kalibangan

Structures commonly described as fire altars were also found in the Harappan occupation at Kalibangan. They are considered possible evidence of ritual activity. The exact beliefs or ceremonies associated with them cannot be established with certainty.

Thus, Kalibangan has 2 different identifying features: crossing agricultural furrows from the earlier occupation and structures interpreted as fire altars associated with Harappan occupation.

Shortughai, Afghanistan: traces of canals

Shortughai was a Harappan settlement in present-day Afghanistan. Archaeologists have identified traces of canals there. Canals are channels constructed or adapted to carry water, including water for agricultural land.

The canal traces are important because they provide site-specific evidence for the management or movement of water. Agricultural settlements in dry regions often required access to stored or diverted water.

Shortughai was also situated near an important source of lapis lazuli, a blue stone valued for ornaments. Its location therefore helps illustrate both agricultural water management and the wider Harappan interest in distant raw materials.

Keep the discoveries separate

Banawali provides evidence in the form of a tool model. Kalibangan provides evidence in the form of marks left in a cultivated field. Shortughai provides evidence in the form of water channels. Each points to a different aspect of agricultural life.

Although traces of canals have been identified at Shortughai, similar canal traces were not identified in the Punjab and Sindh areas discussed in the NCERT account. This does not prove that farmers in those regions never irrigated. Other means of obtaining water, including wells, may have been used.

Prelims focus

  • Banawali, Haryana: terracotta model of a plough.
  • Kalibangan, Rajasthan: Early Harappan ploughed field.
  • Kalibangan's field contains 2 sets of furrows at right angles.
  • Shortughai, Afghanistan: canal traces and proximity to lapis lazuli sources.
  • Kalibangan also has structures interpreted as fire altars.
  • Trap: A clay model of a plough is not the same discovery as an actual field bearing plough marks.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, pp. 3–4, 12, and section 11.2, p. 23; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, p. 96; Directorate of Archaeology and Museums, Government of Haryana, Ancient Site at Banawali, consulted 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Excavations at Kalibangan: The Harappans, Chapter 1, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Evidence of Agriculture and Irrigation: Banawali, Kalibangan and Shortughai

body:
Ropar: a Harappan site on the Sutlej

Ropar, now commonly called Rupnagar, is in present-day Punjab, India, on the bank of the Sutlej River. It was the first Harappan site excavated in independent India, with excavations beginning in 1953.

The site contains remains from the Harappan period and later periods of occupation. This sequence shows that a place may be occupied by different communities over a long span of time, even when their pottery and other objects change.

Important finds at Ropar

Harappan remains from Ropar include a steatite seal, a clay sealing and a cemetery. Excavations of the cemetery provided evidence of Harappan burial practices. A burial involving a human and a dog has also been reported from the site.

A seal is an object, often made of stone, with an engraved design that could be pressed into soft material. A sealing is the resulting impression, commonly left in clay. The 2 terms are related but do not refer to the same object.

Ropar is a site in Punjab, not Haryana. Its location on the Sutlej, Harappan cemetery and seal-related finds are useful identifying clues.

Rakhigarhi: an extensive Harappan settlement in Haryana

Rakhigarhi is situated in present-day Hisar district, Haryana. It is one of the most important Harappan settlement complexes in India and is recognised as the largest known Harappan settlement in official reporting available at the selected content cutoff.

The site has evidence of occupation from the Early Harappan into the Mature Harappan period. Excavations have revealed planned settlement areas, drainage arrangements, craft-production evidence and burial grounds. These discoveries show that Rakhigarhi was more than a small isolated village.

Burials and the dated excavation record

Human burials are an important identifying feature of Rakhigarhi. In a release dated 22 June 2026, India's Ministry of Culture described the settlement as extending over approximately 550 hectares. The release reported that the Archaeological Survey of India had uncovered 8 burials at Mound 7 during the 2025–26 excavation season, including 3 complete human skeletons.

These figures describe the site area and discoveries reported at that date. The number of burials from a particular excavation season must not be mistaken for the total number of burials ever found at Rakhigarhi. The area figure is also an approximate official estimate rather than an unchanging measurement.

How the 2 sites differ

Both sites contain Harappan remains and burial evidence, but they are remembered for different reasons. Ropar connects Harappan settlement with the Sutlej region and the first post-Independence excavation of a Harappan site in India. Rakhigarhi demonstrates the large scale of Harappan settlement in Haryana and preserves evidence from both Early and Mature Harappan occupation.

Neither site should be identified solely by the presence of a burial. Instead, combine its present-day state, geographical setting and distinctive evidence.

Prelims focus

  • Ropar or Rupnagar: Punjab, on the Sutlej River.
  • Ropar was the first Harappan site excavated in independent India.
  • Ropar has Harappan seal-related finds and cemetery remains.
  • Rakhigarhi: Hisar district, Haryana.
  • Rakhigarhi has both Early and Mature Harappan occupation and is recognised as an exceptionally large settlement.
  • Trap: Ropar is in Punjab, while Rakhigarhi is in Haryana.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Fig. 1.22, p. 15; Government of Punjab, Rupnagar District Administration, Archaeological Museum, consulted 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Indian Archaeology 1954–55: A Review, section Rupar, District Ambala; Ministry of Culture, Government of India, Human Skeletal Remains from Rakhigarhi Transferred to Anthropological Survey of India for Advanced Scientific Research, press release dated 22 June 2026.]
